prompt: At a restaurant, $30\%$ of customers order dessert, independently. Of the next $5$ customers, what is the probability that at most $1$ orders dessert? Round to three decimal places.
hint: "At most $1$" allows two outcomes: nobody orders dessert, or exactly one customer does. Each is a binomial probability.

hints.text: "At most $1$" allows two outcomes: nobody orders dessert, or exactly one customer does. Each is a binomial probability.

hints.title: 🪜 Try a simpler one
hints.text: Warm up with 2 customers: $P(0) = 0.7^2 = 0.49$ and $P(1) = 2(0.3)(0.7) = 0.42$, so $P(X \le 1) = 0.91$. Same method with $n = 5$.
With $n = 5$ and $p = 0.3$, find $P(X = 0) = (0.7)^5$ and $P(X = 1) = \binom{5}{1}(0.3)(0.7)^4$, and then add them.
$0.7^5 \approx 0.168$ and $5(0.3)(0.2401) \approx 0.360$, so the probability of at most one dessert order is about $0.528$.

explanation: $X$ is binomial with $n = 5$ and $p = 0.3$, and "at most 1" means $P(X = 0) + P(X = 1)$.
No desserts means all five customers decline: $P(X = 0) = 0.7^5 = 0.16807$.
Exactly one dessert can come from any of the five customers: $P(X = 1) = 5 \times 0.3 \times 0.7^4 = 5 \times 0.3 \times 0.2401 = 0.36015$.
The total is $0.16807 + 0.36015 = 0.52822$, so the probability is about $0.528$.

alternativeExplanations.title: Count the arrangements
steps: Zero desserts: one arrangement (N N N N N), probability $0.7^5 = 0.16807$.
Exactly one dessert: the dessert customer could be any of 5 positions, each arrangement with probability $0.3 \times 0.7^4 = 0.07203$; total $5 \times 0.07203 = 0.36015$.
